parts: Lesson 10: Religious Reform Movements in Modern India — Summary

The Indian society of the first half of the 19th century was caste-ridden, decadent and rigid. The British brought English and modern ideas of liberty, equality, fraternity, democracy and justice. From the late 19th century European and Indian scholars studied ancient India's history, philosophy, science and literature, giving Indians pride and helping reformers. Since social evils had religious links, most social reform movements were religious in character; they arose among all communities, attacked bigotry, superstition and the hold of the priestly class, and worked against caste and untouchability, purdah, sati, child marriage, social inequality and illiteracy; some were supported directly or indirectly by British officials.
Brahmo Samaj and Raja Rammohan Roy

Raja Rammohan Roy combined East and West: he studied Christianity and Islam, wrote in Bengali, English and Persian, and promoted English education. He condemned idol worship, sacrifices and the priestly class, held that the ancient Hindu texts preached monotheism, and in 1828 founded the Brahmo Sabha (Brahmo Samaj): open to all regardless of caste, colour or religion; it forbade idol worship, sacrifices and offerings, forbade attacking any religion, believed in the unity of all religions and emphasised human dignity. He worked against sati – citing the oldest scriptures and appealing to reason and compassion, visiting burning ghats – until it was declared illegal in 1829; he opposed caste, polygamy and child marriage, and wanted women to be educated, to inherit property and widows to remarry. Debendranath Tagore and Keshub Chandra Sen succeeded him; the Samaj stood for individual freedom, national unity and democratisation and was the first organised vehicle of national awakening, but it remained confined to urban educated groups.
Prarthana Samaj, Young Bengal, Vidyasagar and other regions

The Prarthana Samaj (Bombay, founded by Dr Atmaram Pandurang; textbook date 1876, usually given as 1867) aimed at rational worship and social reform – inter-caste dining and marriage, widow remarriage, improvement of the lot of women and depressed classes; R.G. Bhandarkar and Justice M.G. Ranade (founder of the Widow Remarriage Association, Deccan Education Society and Poona Sarvajanik Sabha) were its leaders; it did not insist on a rigid break with idol worship or caste. Henry Derozio (teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta; died of cholera at 22) and the Young Bengal movement questioned all authority and cherished the ideals of the French Revolution. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar got the law permitting widow remarriage passed in 1856 and promoted girls' schools. Western India: Bal Shastri Jambekar attacked Brahmanical orthodoxy; Parmahansa Mandali (1849); Jotiba Phule (girls' school in Poona 1857, school for the depressed classes, called 'Mahatma'). South: Kandukuri Veeresalingam (Andhra, widow remarriage), Veda Samaj (Madras, 1864, Chembeti Sridharalu Naidu), and Shree Narayana Guru (Kerala, 1854–1928) who founded the SNDP Yogam in 1903 and preached 'One caste, one religion, one God'.
Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission, Theosophical Society

Mool Shankar, later Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1824–83) of Gujarat, founded the Arya Samaj at Bombay in 1875: the Vedas contain all knowledge and the essentials of science; opposed idolatry, ritual, priesthood and caste practices; favoured western science; used Hindi; his chief book is Satyarth Prakash. It opposed child marriage and encouraged widow remarriage; it started DAV schools and colleges (the first at Lahore, 1886; Lala Hansraj); Swami Shraddhananda started the Gurukul near Haridwar (1902) to propagate traditional ideas of education; suddhi was a purification ceremony for Hindus converted to Islam or Christianity; it spread self-respect and nationalism, especially in Punjab, UP, Rajasthan and Gujarat. Gadadhar Chattopadhyaya (Ramakrishna Paramahansa, 1836–86) believed there are many roads to God and that service of man is service of God, so there is no sectarianism. Narendranath Datta (Swami Vivekananda, 1863–1902) carried the message to America and Europe, condemned caste and rigid ritual, advocated liberty and free thinking, promoted Vedanta and the oneness of religions, said service to the poor and downtrodden is the highest religion and founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 (social service in famine, floods and epidemics; schools, hospitals and orphanages); at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago (1893) he showed that Vedanta is the religion of all. The Theosophical Society was founded in the USA in 1875 by Madame H.P. Blavatsky (Russian) and Colonel H.S. Olcott (American); it came to India in 1879 and its headquarters were set up at Adyar near Madras in 1886; under Annie Besant it revived ancient religions, taught universal brotherhood, fought untouchability, advocated women's upliftment, founded the Central Hindu College at Banaras (later BHU under Malaviya) and began the Home Rule League in 1916; its journal was the Theosophist.

After 1857 modern reform appeared among Muslims: the Muhammadan Literary Society (Calcutta, 1863, Nawab Abdul Latif), the Chishti Sufis, Shah Waliullah (Delhi), the Firangi Mahal of Lucknow, the Faraizi movement (Shariatullah, Bengal) and Sayyid Ahmed of Rai Bareilly. Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan urged broad-mindedness and tolerance, interpreted the Quran in the light of reason and science, said Hindus and Muslims are 'one nation', had Western books translated into Urdu, and founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in 1875 (later Aligarh Muslim University); the Aligarh Movement aimed to promote modern education without weakening ties with Islam and gave Muslims a common language, Urdu, and a press; he wanted women educated, purdah removed and was against polygamy. The Ahmadiyya movement was founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad in 1899; Muhammad Iqbal was a humanist poet. Parsi reform began in Mumbai in the mid-19th century: the Rehnumai Mazdayasan Sabha (1851) of Naoroji Furdonji, Dadabhai Naoroji, S.S. Bengalee and others and the journal Rast Goftar, promoting girls' education; the Parsis became the most westernised community. Sikh reform began at the end of the 19th century: Singh Sabhas (1870) and, with British support, the Khalsa College at Amritsar (1892) promoted Gurmukhi, Sikh learning and Punjabi; after 1920 the Akali movement sought control of gurdwaras from mahants; a law of 1925 gave management to the Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee.

The British passed few laws to appease orthodoxy: Sati declared illegal (1829), infanticide illegal, widow remarriage permitted (1856), marriageable age of girls raised to ten (1860), inter-caste and inter-communal marriage sanctioned (1872), child marriage discouraged (1891), and the Sharda Act (1929) fixing minimum ages of 14 for girls and 18 for boys. In the 20th century, especially after 1919, the national movement became the main propagator of social reform, using Indian languages, novels, dramas, short stories, poetry, the press and in the 1930s the cinema. Women's education spread, purdah and child marriage declined, women took part in the freedom struggle, and many superstitions disappeared; it was no longer a sin to travel abroad.
